items.title: A p-modular system is a characteristic-zero fraction field over a complete discrete valuation ring with residue field of characteristic p
A splitting p-modular system for a finite group is a p-modular system whose fraction and residue fields split the needed group algebras
An OG-lattice is a finite free module over the valuation ring with G-action, and reduction modulo the maximal ideal produces a kG-module
Reducing an OG-lattice modulo the maximal ideal gives a finite-dimensional kG-module
items.strategy: Reduce a finite free module over the discrete valuation ring modulo its maximal ideal and inherit the G-action through scalar extension to the residue field.

items.title: When the characteristic divides the group order, Maschke can fail and kG need not be semisimple
The Jacobson radical of a finite-dimensional algebra is the intersection of its maximal left ideals
For a finite-dimensional algebra, the Jacobson radical is nilpotent and the quotient by it is semisimple
items.strategy: Use finite length of the regular module to force the descending powers of the radical to terminate, then identify the semisimple quotient by killing the maximal nonsimple obstruction.

items.title: For a finite-dimensional algebra, the module radical is exactly the action of the Jacobson radical
items.strategy: Show that the Jacobson radical annihilates every simple quotient and therefore lands inside the module radical, then pass to the semisimple quotient of the algebra to obtain the reverse inclusion.

items.title: Over a finite-dimensional algebra, a module annihilated modulo its radical is zero, and generators lift from the head
items.strategy: Apply the equality between the module radical and the Jacobson-radical action, then use nilpotence of the algebra radical to bootstrap a radical-stable module equality to vanishing and generator lifting.

items.title: For a finite p-group in characteristic p, the augmentation ideal of the group algebra is nilpotent
items.strategy: Filter the group algebra by the augmentation ideal, use finiteness of the p-group to show the successive quotients terminate, and conclude nilpotence from finite-dimensionality.

items.title: For a finite group and a field of characteristic p, the group algebra is a symmetric Frobenius algebra via the coefficient of the identity
items.strategy: Use the basis of group elements to define the coefficient-of-identity bilinear form and verify associativity, symmetry, and nondegeneracy directly from the multiplication table.

items.title: Over a finite group algebra in defining characteristic, finite-dimensional projective and injective modules coincide
items.strategy: Use the symmetric Frobenius duality to identify the projective and injective lifting-extension tests for finite-dimensional modules over kG.

items.title: The radical, socle, head, and Loewy series of a finite-dimensional module
For a finite-length module, the radical is a superfluous submodule
items.strategy: If a submodule plus the radical already gives the whole module, pass to the head and use semisimplicity there to force the submodule to have been the whole module already.

items.title: An essential epimorphism is a surjection with superfluous kernel, and a projective cover is a projective source with such a map
Every finite-dimensional module has a projective cover, unique up to isomorphism over the target
items.strategy: Start from a free cover, trim it to a minimal projective summand using Nakayama and radical superfluity, then compare two minimal covers by lifting maps both ways and forcing them to be isomorphisms.

items.title: Indecomposable projective kG-modules correspond to simple modules through taking the head
items.strategy: Send an indecomposable projective to its simple head, then recover the projective as the unique projective cover of that simple module.

items.title: Finite-dimensional kG-modules decompose as finite direct sums of indecomposables uniquely up to order and isomorphism
items.strategy: Use finite length to produce an indecomposable decomposition and compare two such decompositions by the usual exchange argument on local endomorphism rings.

items.title: The regular module is a direct sum of the projective covers of the simple modules, with the split-field multiplicities
items.strategy: Decompose the regular module into indecomposable projectives, identify each summand by its simple head, and read the multiplicities from the split-field endomorphism dimensions.

items.title: For a finite group and a field of characteristic p, the group algebra is local exactly when the group is a p-group
items.strategy: For a p-group, identify the augmentation ideal as a nilpotent maximal ideal. Conversely, if kG is local, quotient by a maximal normal p-subgroup and use the existence of a prime-to-p simple quotient to rule out non-p-groups.

items.title: A finite p-group has only the trivial simple module over a field of characteristic p
items.strategy: If kP is local, it has a unique simple module, and the augmentation map shows that the trivial module is one such simple.

items.title: A normal p-subgroup acts trivially on every simple module in characteristic p
items.strategy: Restrict a simple kG-module to the normal p-subgroup, use the local p-group algebra to identify only the trivial simple constituent there, and then observe that the trivial-fixed subspace is G-stable by normality.

items.title: Restriction and induction along a subgroup preserve projective modules
items.strategy: Use Frobenius reciprocity for induction and restriction, together with the explicit free-transversal description of kG over kH, to transfer the lifting property across both functors.

items.title: A module is relatively H-projective when it is a direct summand of one induced from H
Higman's criterion characterizes relative projectivity through the relative trace idempotent test
items.strategy: Compare splitting as an induced summand with the image of the relative trace map on module endomorphisms and show each condition manufactures the other.

items.title: A vertex is a minimal p-subgroup for relative projectivity, and a source is an indecomposable inducing summand there
Vertices exist for indecomposable modules, are conjugate in G, and sources are conjugate by the appropriate normalizer
items.strategy: Choose a minimal p-subgroup witnessing relative projectivity, compare two such choices through restriction-induction decompositions, and then apply indecomposable uniqueness to force conjugacy.

items.title: A projective indecomposable module has trivial vertex
items.strategy: Projective modules are already relatively 1-projective, so minimality in the vertex definition forces the trivial subgroup.

items.title: If the field has characteristic p and p divides |G|, then Maschke's theorem still makes kG semisimple
items.strategy: Use the standard nonsemisimple Cp-module in characteristic p, or equivalently the nonsemisimplicity of kG itself, to contradict the claim immediately.

items.title: Every reduction modulo p of an ordinary irreducible lattice stays irreducible
items.strategy: Reduce an integral S3-lattice in characteristic three and observe that the resulting module has a nontrivial composition series.

items.title: A module has one literally canonical projective cover, not just a unique isomorphism class over the target
items.strategy: Compare two isomorphic projective covers obtained from different minimal projective summands of a free cover: uniqueness is only up to isomorphism commuting with the cover map.

items.title: The vertex of an indecomposable module is literally a graph vertex of a Cayley graph
items.strategy: A module vertex is a subgroup chosen by a relative projectivity condition, not a point of a graph, so the statement confuses two unrelated meanings of the same word.

items.title: Projective and injective modules coincide over every ring
items.strategy: The coincidence on this page uses the symmetric Frobenius structure of finite-dimensional group algebras, so a general ring has no such reason to identify the two notions.

title: Modular Representations and Projective Covers - Examples

items.title: The regular module of Cp in characteristic p is indecomposable with a unique simple quotient
The augmentation ideal and Loewy series of kCp can be written explicitly
For a finite p-group, the augmentation map from kP to the trivial module is its projective cover
Reducing a standard integral lattice for S3 modulo 3 produces a reducible kS3-module
A permutation-induced summand is detected as relatively projective by Higman's criterion
An ordinary irreducible representation can have reducible reduction modulo p

title: Pro P Groups and the P Adic Integers

items.title: A pro-p group is a profinite group that is an inverse limit of finite p-groups
The pro-p completion of an abstract group is the inverse limit over its finite p-group quotients
A topological group is pro-p exactly when it is profinite and has an open normal basis with finite p-group quotients
items.strategy: Specialize the profinite characterization to inverse systems whose finite quotients are p-groups, and read the converse from the neighborhood-basis quotients.

items.title: The p-adic integers are the compatible residue-class tuples in the inverse limit of Z mod p^n
Coordinatewise addition and negation make Zp a topological abelian group
items.strategy: Check compatibility of residue-class representatives coordinatewise and inherit continuity from the product topology on the inverse-limit model.

items.title: The p-adic metric on Zp is determined by the first coordinate at which two compatible residue systems differ
The inverse-limit topology on Zp agrees with the p-adic metric topology
items.strategy: Identify the basic metric balls with the kernels of the coordinate projections and compare them with the standard cylinder neighborhoods of the inverse limit.

items.title: Zp is Hausdorff, totally disconnected, and complete, and compact assuming Choice
items.strategy: Use the inverse-limit description for compactness and total disconnectedness, then transfer completeness through the equality of the inverse-limit and p-adic metric topologies.

items.title: The canonical map from Z to Zp sends an integer to its coherent residue classes modulo p^n
The canonical map from the integers into Zp is injective and has dense image
items.strategy: Injectivity is divisibility by every p-power, while density is coordinatewise surjectivity onto every finite stage of the inverse system.

items.title: The additive group of Zp is torsion-free
items.strategy: If a nonzero p-adic integer had finite additive order, look at the first nonzero residue digit and reduce the relation modulo a sufficiently high power of p.

items.title: The additive topological group of Zp is topologically generated by 1, although it is not abstractly cyclic
items.strategy: Use density of the embedded integers together with the fact that every integer multiple of 1 already lies in the image of Z.

items.title: Zp is the pro-p completion of the integers
items.strategy: Identify the inverse system defining Zp with the cofinal system of p-power-index quotients of Z and invoke the universal property of inverse limits.

items.title: The profinite completion of the integers is the direct product of the p-adic integer groups over all primes
items.strategy: Apply the Chinese remainder theorem to the finite quotients and pass to the inverse limit over all moduli by cofinality.

items.title: The Frattini subgroup of a profinite group is the intersection of its maximal proper closed subgroups
Every maximal proper closed subgroup of a profinite group is open
items.strategy: Pass to the compact Hausdorff quotient by the subgroup and use profiniteness to show that maximal proper closed quotients are finite simple and therefore discrete.

items.title: For surjective inverse systems in the pro-p setting, the Frattini subgroup commutes with the inverse limit
items.strategy: Use surjectivity of the transition maps to track maximal open subgroups through the inverse system and identify the limit Frattini subgroup coordinatewise.

items.title: For a finitely generated pro-p group, the Frattini subgroup is the closure of [G,G]G^p
items.strategy: Pass to finite p-group quotients, apply the finite Frattini formula there, and then recover the closed subgroup in the inverse limit.

items.title: A subset topologically generates a finitely generated pro-p group exactly when its image spans the Frattini quotient over Fp
items.strategy: Reduce the generation question to every finite p-group quotient, apply the ordinary Burnside basis theorem there, and then reassemble the conclusion through the pro-p Frattini formula.

items.title: A homomorphism of finitely generated pro-p groups is surjective exactly when the induced map on Frattini quotients is surjective
items.strategy: Apply the topological Burnside basis theorem to the image of the homomorphism inside the target group.

items.title: Zp is the full profinite completion of the integers
items.strategy: Compare Zp with the product decomposition of the full profinite completion and note that the prime-to-p quotients are missing.

items.title: Because every coordinate group is finite, Zp is an additive torsion group
items.strategy: A finite-coordinate inverse limit can still be torsion-free, and Zp itself provides the witness.

items.title: The additive group of Zp is cyclic as an abstract group
items.strategy: Topological generation by one only gives density of the integer multiples; abstract cyclicity would force every element literally to be an integer multiple of 1.

items.title: For a finitely generated pro-p group, the Frattini subgroup equals [G,G]G^p
items.strategy: The pro-p Frattini formula lands in the closure of the abstract subgroup generated by commutators and pth powers, and the closure is part of the statement rather than a cosmetic add-on.

items.title: Every profinite group is pro-p for some prime
items.strategy: Take a profinite group with quotients of at least two different prime-power types, such as the full profinite completion of Z.

title: Pro P Groups and the P Adic Integers - Examples

items.title: A p-adic integer is encoded by a compatible sequence of residue digits
The partial sums of a p-adic expansion converge in the inverse-limit topology
A standard p-adic digit sequence is Cauchy and converges in Zp
A finite p-group is naturally isomorphic to its own pro-p completion
The Frattini quotient of Zp is the one-dimensional vector space Fp
In Zp squared, topological generation is detected by the Frattini quotient coordinates
The embedded integers form an abstractly proper but topologically dense subgroup of Zp
